implementation_notes: Go's assignment already gives a value copy, so a struct whose fields are all values is its own memento - `snapshot := editor.state` captures an independent state, and a slice or ring buffer of those values is the caretaker. Fields that are references (slices, maps, pointers) keep sharing their backing storage, so the originator must clone them explicitly with slices.Clone and maps.Clone, both of which are shallow by contract; nested references need their own clones, or the state should be reshaped into immutable values. The classic interface/opaque-memento structure is unnecessary in Go because the snapshot can be an ordinary exported value type that only the originator builds and interprets.
pitfalls: A value copy still shares slice, map and pointer fields: appending to the live slice may or may not reallocate, so a snapshot can pass small tests and mutate under production load.
slices.Clone and maps.Clone are shallow by contract - nested slices, maps and pointers stay shared between the original and the copy.

Copying a struct that contains a sync.Mutex, sync.Once or another lock (go vet's copylocks check flags this) duplicates the lock rather than the protected state; keep lockable state outside the snapshot.
A growing history slice keeps every version alive and can dominate memory; use a ring buffer with a fixed capacity.

variants.name: Serialized round-trip snapshots (encoding/gob, encoding/json)
variants.idiom_name: gob or JSON encode/decode into a detached snapshot
variants.implementation_notes: When the snapshot must be fully detached from any alias, persisted, or shipped to another process, serialize instead of copying: gob encodes exported struct fields recursively, handles maps, slices and pointers, and decoding allocates a fresh object graph, while encoding/json does the same for JSON-compatible state at the cost of type fidelity. The caretaker stores bytes or decoded values and undo writes the value back through the originator. Choose gob for Go-to-Go durable history and JSON when snapshots are inspected, diffed or exchanged with other systems; for hot in-memory undo, the value-copy variant is faster and allocation-friendlier.
pitfalls: gob encodes exported fields only and needs concrete types registered (gob.Register) for interface values, so unexported state silently disappears from the snapshot.
Every undo allocates and decodes a fresh graph, adding CPU and GC pressure - use serialized history for durable checkpoints, not per-keystroke undo.
JSON round-trips lose Go type information (numbers become float64 in map[string]any, named numeric types decay), so it is a poor choice when restoration must be exact.
